lead: At 11 km the air outside is thin and cold: a crew cannot breathe it, because the lungs cannot take enough oxygen out of it. So the cabin is sealed and fed with conditioned air, while a valve at the rear lets the surplus out at a controlled rate. That valve, not the supply, sets the cabin pressure. On most airliners the supply is hot bleed air, so a pack cools it and then expands it through a turbine.
prereq: You need: the bleed air source and its regulation from Chapter 2.2.

sections.h3: Why the cabin must hold a pressure altitude

blocks.text: At 35 000 ft the air outside is at about 23.8 kPa, against 101.3 kPa at sea level. Oxygen is still 21 % of the air, so its partial pressure falls from about 21.3 kPa to 5.0 kPa, and the blood can no longer load enough of it. The result is hypoxia: dulled judgement first, then loss of consciousness.

Trapped gas is the second problem. By Boyle’s law pV is constant, so one litre of gas in the middle ear, a sinus or the gut at 101.3 kPa becomes 101.3 ÷ 23.8 = 4.3 litres at 35 000 ft, which causes pain and can damage tissue.

So the cabin is held at a cabin altitude: the altitude in the standard atmosphere whose pressure equals the cabin pressure. The usual limit is 8000 ft (2438 m), where the pressure is 75.3 kPa. The fuselage sets a maximum differential pressure, typically about 55–60 kPa (8–9 psi) on an airliner.
Δp = p<sub>cabin</sub> − p<sub>ambient</sub>        F = Δp × A
blocks.where: Δp is the differential pressure in Pa; F is the outward force in N on a panel of area A in m².

blocks.text: At cruise the cabin sits near 8000 ft and Δp is large, so the hull carries a heavy steady load. If the cabin cannot hold its pressure, the cabin altitude rises and the crew must act; oxygen for that case is in aircraft oxygen systems.

sections.h3: The outflow valve sets the pressure

blocks.text: The fuselage is a pressure vessel with doors and many seals, and it is never airtight. Air enters from the packs at a controlled mass flow and leaves through the outflow valve, a motor-driven gate near the rear. Open it and cabin pressure falls; close it and pressure rises.

The cabin pressure controller reads cabin pressure from its own sensors, takes static pressure from the air data system, and drives the valve to follow a schedule. The crew selects a target cabin altitude and a rate of change, or lets the automatic schedule fly it.

items: Ground: valve fully open, cabin at field elevation, no differential.
Takeoff: the valve closes a little after liftoff, so the cabin does not bump.
Climb: cabin altitude rises at a limited rate, a few hundred feet per minute, towards 8000 ft.
Descent: the cabin comes down so that it reaches field elevation at touchdown.
Manual: the crew drives the valve directly if the automatic channels fail.

blocks.text: Three protections sit outside the controller. The positive pressure relief (safety) valve opens outward if Δp passes the structural limit. The negative pressure relief valve opens inward if outside pressure is higher than inside, for example in a fast descent with the outflow valve shut. A dump function drives the outflow valve fully open: in flight it clears smoke or fumes, and on the ground it brings the cabin to field pressure so the doors can be opened.

sections.h3: Air cycle cooling: expand the air and it cools

blocks.text: Bleed air reaches the pack at roughly 200 °C and 2 to 3 bar. The pack uses no refrigerant; it uses the air itself. Three effects share the work: heat transfer to ram air, compression and expansion. Air cycle cooling is light, needs no refrigerant, and the same air also pressurises and ventilates the cabin; its cost is the bleed air taken from the engines.

items: Flow control valve: meters bleed air and holds the pack to its design mass flow.
Primary heat exchanger: ram air from a scoop removes heat.
Compressor: raises the pressure again. The air gets hotter, but the higher pressure ratio lets the turbine extract more work and cool it further.
Secondary heat exchanger: ram air removes the compression heat, bringing the air back near ram-air temperature at a higher pressure.
Turbine: the air expands and does work on the wheel, which drives the compressor on the same shaft. It leaves very cold, near 0 °C or below.
Water separator: condensed water is spun or coalesced out, so no fog or ice reaches the cabin.

blocks.text: Why does expansion cool? In the turbine the air hands over energy as shaft work, so its temperature drops steeply; air forced through a plain hole keeps its energy and hardly cools. For an ideal (isentropic) turbine:

blocks.where: T is absolute temperature in K, p is absolute pressure, 1 is the turbine inlet, 2 the outlet, and γ = 1.4 for air. A real turbine of efficiency η gives T₂ = T₁ − η(T₁ − T₂s).

blocks.text: In the bootstrap cycle, the one above, the turbine drives the compressor. In the simple cycle there is no compressor: the turbine drives a fan that pulls cooling air through the heat exchanger. It gives less cooling and suits small aircraft and low demand.

The pack delivers air colder than needed. Hot trim air from the bleed is mixed back in through trim valves to hold each zone at its selected temperature. On the ground a fan on the air cycle machine shaft pulls ram air through the heat exchangers; in flight a modulating inlet flap sets the ram flow.

examples.question: An aircraft cruises at 35 000 ft, where the ambient pressure is 23.8 kPa. The cabin is held at 8000 ft, where the pressure is 75.3 kPa. (a) Find the differential pressure in kPa and in psi. (b) Find the outward force on a plug-type door of area 1.2 m². Take 1 psi = 6.895 kPa.
steps: List the data: p_cabin = 75.3 kPa, p_ambient = 23.8 kPa, A = 1.2 m².
Convert to base units: 51.5 kPa = 51 500 Pa.
examples.answer: Differential pressure 51.5 kPa (7.47 psi); outward force on the door 61.8 kN.

examples.question: Air enters a pack’s cooling turbine at 300 kPa and 40 °C and leaves at 80 kPa. Take γ = 1.4. Find the outlet temperature for an ideal turbine and for a turbine of efficiency 0.80.
examples.answer: About −58 °C for an ideal turbine and −39 °C for the real one; the pack then mixes in warm trim air so the cabin supply is not too cold.

traps: Saying the pack compressor cools the air. It heats it. The turbine cools it, because the air gives up shaft work there.
Saying the supply pressure sets the cabin pressure. The outflow valve sets it; the supply only has to cover the leak plus the outflow.
Mixing cabin altitude with aircraft altitude: the cabin is at 8000 ft while the aircraft is at 35 000 ft.
Unit slips in Δp × A: kPa must become Pa (× 1000) before multiplying by area in m², or the force comes out 1000 times too small; and the turbine formula needs kelvin, not °C.
Reversing the relief valves. The positive relief valve opens outward on excess Δp; the negative relief valve opens inward when outside pressure wins.

quiz.q: State the usual maximum cabin altitude and the pressure that goes with it.
quiz.a: 8000 ft (2438 m), where the standard-atmosphere pressure is 75.3 kPa.

quiz.q: An aircraft is at 30 000 ft (p = 30.1 kPa) with the cabin at 6000 ft (p = 81.2 kPa). Find Δp and the outward force on a window of area 0.8 m².
The outflow valve jams closed in cruise. What happens to Δp, which valve protects the structure, and what should the crew do?
quiz.a: The packs keep pumping air in and only the small leaks let it out, so cabin pressure and Δp rise. When Δp reaches the safety setting the positive pressure relief valve opens and holds it at the limit. The crew uses the manual mode to drive the outflow valve, or reduces pack flow, and before landing makes sure the cabin is depressurised so the doors can be opened.

quiz.q: Where is the water taken out in a low-pressure and in a high-pressure water separation pack?
quiz.a: In a low-pressure pack the separator is after the turbine, where the air is coldest and the water has condensed. In a high-pressure pack a condenser and water extractor sit before the turbine, so dry air enters it and the turbine can run below 0 °C without icing.

quiz.q: A type has a maximum differential pressure of 55 kPa and holds the cabin at 75.3 kPa. At what ambient pressure is the limit reached, and what must the controller do above that altitude?
quiz.a: p_ambient = 75.3 − 55 = 20.3 kPa. Above the altitude where ambient pressure is 20.3 kPa, the controller must let the cabin altitude rise with the aircraft so that Δp stays at the limit; the cabin can no longer be held at 8000 ft.

beyond: Not for the exam. The Boeing 787 takes no bleed air for the cabin: electric compressors feed its packs, and it holds a lower cabin altitude, near 6000 ft. Search for "bleedless environmental control system" and "cabin air quality".
